name: Okinawa diet

card.summary: The traditional low-calorie, plant-heavy Ryukyu eating pattern, followed by people interested in lean, healthy, youthful-looking aging.
card.note: Traditional version was low in protein, fat and some B vitamins.

quick.overview:
The Okinawa diet describes how people in the Ryukyu Islands traditionally ate: mostly sweet potato, with vegetables, soy foods such as tofu and miso, seaweed and small amounts of fish or pork. Calorie intake was lower than the Japanese average.

People adopt it for leanness, healthy aging and the long lifespans Okinawa was known for. Observational data link the traditional pattern to low rates of several diseases, though researchers note that low calorie intake and activity, not diet alone, may explain the longevity.
quick.how: In practice people shift toward vegetables, sweet potato or other whole carbohydrates, soy foods and seaweed, with little sugar and meat; the related Okinawan habit of "hara hachi bu" (eating to about 80% fullness) is often paired with it.
quick.risks: The traditional pattern was low in some nutrients; Okinawan surveys noted cheilosis, likely from low riboflavin. Okinawa's life-expectancy lead has since narrowed as diets westernized.

lead: The Okinawa diet is the traditional eating pattern of the Ryukyu Islands, centred on sweet potato, which supplied about 69% of calories around 1950, with smaller shares from rice, other grains, soy and legumes, and green and yellow vegetables.[1]

People pursue it as a route to a lean body and to healthy aging, which shows in skin and overall appearance. Okinawans of the period ate less overall (about 1,785 kcal versus 2,068 for other Japanese) and much less fish, meat and sugar.[1]

Research is mostly observational: life expectancy in the islands from 1949 to 1998 was reported at 83.8 years, and 1995 mortality comparisons found far lower coronary disease and several cancer deaths than in Americans.[1] Reviews of healthy-aging nutrition list the Okinawa diet among patterns linked to better outcomes in older adults.[2]

chain: Little weight gain with age, low BMI
angle.text: The pattern is low in calories and rich in vegetables and soy. Proponents use it to stay lean and support healthy aging; the link to appearance runs through body weight and general health.

infobox: Soy, vegetables, seaweed, small amounts of fish and pork

paras: Besides sweet potato, the traditional diet included tofu and miso soup, seaweed such as wakame, and small amounts of fish, noodles or lean meat, with pork eaten occasionally.[1]
The traditional diet was widely followed until about the 1960s; afterwards fat intake rose from roughly 6% to 27% of calories and rice and bread replaced sweet potato.[1]

Evidence consists of population comparisons and reviews rather than randomized trials of the diet. Mortality comparisons for 1995 found Okinawans about 8 times less likely to die of coronary artery disease and 7 times less likely to die of prostate cancer than Americans of the same age.[1] A 2023 review of nutrition and healthy aging includes the Okinawa diet among beneficial patterns.[2]

Writers on the topic note that calorie restriction and physical activity may be main contributors to the longevity, and that no food has been shown to have anti-aging properties.[1] Since the early 2000s Okinawa's advantage has shrunk, with westernization linked to rising cardiovascular disease.[1] Over 10% had cheilosis, likely from low riboflavin.[1]

timeline.event: Sweet potato supplies about 69% of calories.[1]
Traditional diet declines as Western patterns take hold.[1]
National survey finds Okinawan adults eating 83% of the calories of other Japanese adults.[1]
